slides.title: The Creative Engineer
slides.subtitle: When the cost of building collapses, the value of knowing what to build rises.

slides.title: 161 minutes against 71
slides.lead: In 2022 a team at Microsoft Research ran a randomized controlled experiment on professional developers. One task: write an HTTP server in JavaScript. Half got GitHub Copilot.
slides.why: the chapter opens with two measured magnitudes on one axis — 'The control group finished in 161 minutes. The treatment group finished in 71 minutes. That is a 56% reduction in task completion time.'

slides.title: Wrong reaction: "engineers got more productive"
slides.lead: That is a question about individual performance. I want you to sit with a different one.
bullets: *What exactly got cheaper, and what does that do to the market?*
The first question is about performance. The second is about **market structure**.
This chapter is about the second — and to answer it I have to take you to a **1973 paper in labor economics** that has almost nothing to do with software and almost everything to do with your career.

slides.title: Spence: a signal works only as long as its cost-structure holds
slides.lead: Employers cannot observe productivity. So they use signals — things that correlate with the thing they cannot see.
bullets: A degree signals productive capacity **not** because the courses cause it, but because getting one is *costly* in a way that correlates with capacity.
The signal carries information **because it is hard to fake cheaply.**
Good state — a **separating equilibrium**: the signal sorts high-productivity candidates from lower.
Cost-structure collapses — a **pooling equilibrium**: everyone looks the same on the credential, and the employer is back to guessing.

slides.title: The signal did not vanish. It pooled.
slides.lead: In 2010, "I have a working app on GitHub" cost you version control, a language, a framework, a deployment environment, and something that broke at 11pm — six weekends of genuine work.
bullets: That cost correlated with productive engineering capacity. Recruiters used GitHub the way they used GPA.
The **2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey** found **82%** of developers using AI tools for code. These are not early adopters at the frontier. **They are the population.**
GitHub launched in **2004**. Copilot in **2021**. Peng et al. published in **2023**. The collapse compressed fast.
A repository no longer tells a recruiter whether they are looking at six weekends of craft or a Tuesday afternoon with an LLM.

slides.title: What is still costly after AI tooling?
slides.lead: Sort the work honestly. The chapter names which side each falls on — it never counts them, and neither will this slide.
slides.why: the chapter asks 'what is still costly after AI tooling?' and sorts the work into two named buckets — the threshold demonstration that cheapened, against identifying a problem worth solving, positioning for an audience, and shipping to real users

a CS degree as a sorting credential

data.note: These require human contact with reality. They cannot be prompted away.

slides.title: The new separating signals are the ones AI did not make cheap
slides.lead: The labor-market evidence is consistent with the mechanism.
bullets: Recent analyses of AI engineering salaries report base compensation averaging around **$206,000**.
Specialists pull **30–50% above generalists** at the same seniority level.
That is a market paying for what stayed expensive — not for the ability to produce the pooled signal faster.

slides.title: Ideate · Build · Brand · Ship
slides.lead: The Creative Engineer is an engineer who has noticed the costly signals shifted, and has invested accordingly.
bullets: **Ideate** — the hardest move, and the one generative AI cannot do for you. It will build any specification; it cannot decide whether the specification is worth building.
**Build** — the verb AI cheapened. Necessary. *Not sufficient.* Production systems still need deep technical judgment; what stopped separating is the repo as demonstration.
**Brand** — audience, positioning, archetype, voice, visual identity: whether a stranger in your target audience can find your work and recognize why it is for them.
**Ship** — a public URL, an audience that found it, feedback from real use. Not committed. Not published. Not demoed in class.

slides.title: An API without documentation is technically complete
slides.lead: Brand is where the most resistance lives among technically trained students. Here is the engineering analogy.
bullets: It does the computation. It returns the right values. But if the developer who needs it cannot understand what it is for, **it is useless**.
Documentation is not decoration on the API — it is the part that makes the API connectable to the world that needs it.
**Brand is documentation for your career.**
The common objection is that your work should speak for itself. The honest response: *your work cannot speak at all if the person it is for cannot find it.*

slides.title: The rubric has a direction, and it ends at an artifact
slides.lead: One to five, per verb. A score of 4 on Build with no deployed product is not valid — the score must reflect observable artifacts.
slides.why: the chapter's rubric is an explicitly ordered scale: 'Score 1 — no evidence · Score 3 — some evidence · Score 5 — clear public artifact', with the reader's own score left to them

slides.lead: Anthropic was started by former OpenAI researchers. Both publish frontier research. Both hit competitive capability benchmarks. What is radically different is Brand.
slides.why: the chapter states a shared origin that separates at a named moment — 'Two companies, similar technical work, very different market positions. Brand carved out two audiences that could each sustain a viable company.'

slides.title: Every archetype comes with a shadow
slides.lead: Mark and Pearson adapted Jung into twelve: Hero, Sage, Explorer, Innocent, Creator, Ruler, Caregiver, Magician, Lover, Jester, Everyman, Rebel. Two things going for it here.
bullets: It answers the question you are actually trying to answer — *who am I to the people I am trying to reach?* Not "what can I do." That is skill.
**Hero** → recklessness dressed as determination. **Sage** → analysis without action. **Creator** → perfectionism that never ships. **Explorer** → unfinished repositories.
The shadows are **predictive**: once you identify your archetype, the shadow tells you which failure mode to watch for.
What the framework does *not* do is tell you which to choose. The archetype is **descriptive before it is prescriptive** — you are identifying one already latent in how you work.

slides.title: Evidence-based, not introspective
slides.lead: You are not trying to decide what you wish you were. You are looking at work you have already produced and finding the pattern. Four lenses.
bullets: **Read your public writing.** The archetype is audible in the voice before it is legible in the content.
**Look at the projects you chose** — not what you built for class, but what you built because you wanted to. Project choices reveal motivation.
**Find the negative space.** What is absent tells you as much as what is present. The Sage does not post hot takes; the Rebel rarely posts polished tutorials.
**Name the shadow.** Look for it in your own work history, not in your self-description.

slides.title: Two engineers, read from evidence
slides.lead: Engineer A reads as Rebel — drawn to what is broken, competent through critique, no teaching anywhere. Engineer B reads as Everyman — accessibility framing consistent across every channel.
slides.why: the chapter applies its four evidence lenses across two named cases and then hands the same method to the reader; it names A's negative space explicitly but never names B's, and it never runs the method on you

slides.title: Three frames, one argument
slides.lead: Spence, the four verbs, and the archetypes are not three independent frameworks. They are one argument at three levels of resolution.
slides.why: the chapter states an explicit dependency stack — Spence explains *why* the market shifted, the four verbs explain *what* the new costly signals are, the archetype explains *how* to execute Brand — and names what breaks without each

edges.label: a role, not a style choice

slides.section: the bet, stated as a bet
slides.title: What would change my mind
slides.lead: A controlled study showing that, holding technical skill constant, brand-strategy and positioning skills do *not* predict career outcomes for AI engineers.
slides.why: the chapter registers a commitment before the evidence arrives and says so outright — 'The data is not there yet in either direction. The bet here is that the current trajectory continues. That is a bet, not a proof.'

data.axisLabel: the falsification test — designed, not run

slides.title: Madison drafts the baseline. You assign the scores.
slides.lead: Pull your public footprint into one table. Draft the scoring scaffold. Surface which verb your evidence is thinnest on. Then stop.
slides.why: the chapter's AI+1 block enumerates a permission boundary directly — three things AI does well, and three named crossings under 'When NOT to Use AI', each with a stated failure reason

slides.title: Why brand work feels like a category violation
slides.lead: Technically excellent practitioners refuse this work even when shown the labor-market evidence.
bullets: Some of it is identity — *"I am an engineer, not a marketer."* Some of it is sunk cost — years of training for signals that are now depreciating.
But there is a third thing I do not fully understand. Project management does not trigger this. Brand does.
I suspect it has to do with the difference between **making** something and **claiming** something — and a specific anxiety that claiming distorts the making.
The violation feeling is real even when the resistance is unjustified. *That is worth more thought than I have given it here.*

slides.title: Score yourself. Then open the artifact you cited.
slides.lead: Every grey slot on this deck is yours: which verb your evidence is thinnest on, which archetype your negative space actually confirms, and whether the bet in this chapter survives a study nobody has run yet. Treat an unverifiable claim as false — including your own.
